One potential across the three regimes

The same real potential V(E) is used for bound states (E < 0), Gamow states (0 < E < VB) and scattering. Absorption W(E) is switched on only above its onset energy EW.

V(r, E, ℓ) = −V₀ (1 − βE) (1 + cM(−1)ℓ) f(r; RV, aV) W(E) = W₀ (E − EW)² / [(E − EW)² + ΔW²], E > EW

Bound and quasi-bound (Gamow) states

Bands of fixed Wildermuth number G = 2n + ℓ. Each state is solved self-consistently, E = Epole[V(E)]. At a resonance this is the complex-energy condition, so widths include the energy-dependence factor 1/N, N = 1 − ⟨∂V/∂E⟩.

A · Continuous (Igo) ambiguity: the elastic χ² valley

For each shift ΔrV the depth V₀ (and optionally W₀) is refitted to the current elastic distribution. Potentials along the valley fit elastic scattering about equally well. The tracked bound or quasi-bound state shows which member the spectrum selects.

B · Discrete ambiguity: depth families

At fixed geometry, depths that place state (ℓ, n) at the same energy form discrete families. They differ by one interior node per family, and the Wildermuth condition G = 2n + ℓ selects one.

Pseudo-data generator (closure tests)

Generates observables from the current potential, treated as the truth, with a seeded noise model. Positive observables (σ/σR, σR, Γ, ANC, B(E2)) get log-normal noise; energies and phase shifts get Gaussian noise. Energy uncertainties act as model-error floors.

Add data

Angular distributions from the IAEA exfortables_py collection (derived from EXFOR) on GitHub, which allows cross-origin requests. Find the datasets first, then load the ones you select. Listings are cached for a week, because GitHub allows 60 unauthenticated listing requests per hour.

—

Tick the cluster-band members and give each its Wildermuth band G (ℓ = J for a spin-zero cluster on a 0⁺ core; n = (G − ℓ)/2). Levels with similar Jπ can belong to different bands, so check the assignment against the literature before using it.

NUBASE2020 α-decay data (Kondev et al., Chin. Phys. C 45, 030001 (2021)), the table carried by gamow.html. The decay energy fixes the energy of the quasi-bound state. The partial half-life adds information only through the preformation factor Pα, so it needs a prior on Pα or ratios between emitters.

—

Rows

Nuisance parameters

One multiplicative factor φ per group: data normalisations (norm), preformation or reduced-width factors (pre: Γ ∝ φ, T½ ∝ 1/φ) and spectroscopic factors (sf: ANC ∝ √φ). Each factor is profiled exactly in log space, as free, with a log-normal prior, or fixed.

Model-error floors

Added in quadrature to each datum: σeff² = σ² + abs² + (rel·|y|)². They stand for what the two-body model cannot describe and stop keV-precise energies from dominating χ².

Registry versus the current potential

Model values for every included row, the nuisance factors profiled, and the χ² by observable class. Stage 3 builds the sensitivity matrix on these same rows.

Sensitivity matrix and observable → parameter assignment

Derivatives of every included registry row (tab 7) with respect to the free potential parameters, taken at the potential in the left panel. Each row is whitened by its effective uncertainty (σ combined with the model-error floor); positive observables are compared in log space. Nuisance factors (normalisations, Pα, θ², S) are profiled out exactly, which is the Schur complement of the nuisance block. The Fisher matrix F = JᵀJ then gives the local covariance C = F⁻¹ of the potential parameters.

Free parameters (derivatives are computed for these)
Fill the registry (tab 7, or tab 5 → Send to registry), choose the free parameters and press Compute. Cost: 1 + 2 × (number of parameters) forward evaluations of the registry, twice that with the h/2 check.

Parameters

σ is the local 1σ uncertainty from C = F⁻¹ with all listed parameters free. Share is the fraction of Var(p) that a class supplies: Wcj = Σi∈c (C Ji)j² / Cjj, and each column sums to 1. The assigned class comes from the one-to-one assignment that maximises the total share (Hungarian algorithm). Pivot order is the column-pivoted QR order, i.e. the order in which a sequential fit would fix the parameters.

Re-analyse with only these free (the others fixed, no new derivatives)

Sensitivity S, log₁₀

Whitened derivatives summed in quadrature over each class, per unit of the parameter scale (relative for V₀, r, a, W₀; absolute 10⁻³ MeV⁻¹ for β and 0.01 for cM). S ignores correlations; W includes them.

Eigen-directions of F

Each column is one eigen-direction, labelled by its width 1/√λ in scaled units. The leftmost is the least constrained combination.

Igo direction and linearity

The Igo direction keeps VN(rs) fixed at fixed aV: d ln V₀ = −g d ln rV, with g = d ln f(rs)/d ln rV. The check below recomputes the exact χ² of the registry along the least constrained eigen-direction and along the Igo line, in steps of their linear width, and compares it with the quadratic prediction. Agreement means the Fisher σ can be trusted. A χ² that flattens means a long curved valley: use the exact constraint map (tab 10), the family scan (Stage 4) or profile likelihoods (Stage 5).

Information ladder

Cumulative analysis with the derivatives already computed: start with one class of observables and add the next. Each step shows how σ, ρ(V₀, rV) and the width along the Igo line change.

Method and limitations

  • Derivatives are central differences with steps 10⁻³ (relative) for V₀, r, a, W₀, EW, ΔW; 10⁻⁵ MeV⁻¹ for β; 10⁻³ for cM. The pole cache of the central point warm-starts both sides. The h/2 check repeats every column at half the step and reports the largest row-normalised change.
  • Fixed nuisance factors shift the residuals. Free factors are projected out of the Jacobian. Prior factors add one pseudo-row (1/σprior) before projection.
  • The analysis is local, a linearisation at the current potential. When the potential is far from the best fit, or along curved valleys such as the Igo family, σ and the shares describe only the neighbourhood of that point. The linearity check above shows how far the description holds.
  • The information budget is a variance decomposition, not a causal statement. A small share means the parameter is fixed jointly by several classes, not that the class is useless.
  • V₀ and W₀ are moved as p₀ ex in the linearity check and the map, and the other parameters as p₀ + x s. Both mappings give the same Jacobian, but the Igo family is nearly straight in (ln V₀, rV).

Constraint map

Shows where each observable class confines a pair of potential parameters. Each class is drawn at its Δχ² level with the other parameters held at the current values; one of them can be offset. In linear mode the classes come from the sensitivity matrix of tab 9: instant, but local. The dashed ellipse is the joint constraint with all other free parameters profiled. In exact mode χ² is recomputed with the forward model at every grid point, with nuisance factors profiled within each class. Exact mode is needed for curved valleys such as the Igo family.

Compute the sensitivity in tab 9 first; the map uses its parameters, classes and rows.

Classes on the map

Discrete-family scan χ²(V₀)

V₀ is stepped over the chosen range. At each value the selected free parameters are refitted (Levenberg–Marquardt) to the rows of the selected classes, with nuisance factors profiled as in tab 8. Each class is then evaluated at the fitted potential, so the per-class curves show which observables select a family. Every point is labelled by the family coordinate ν of the band head, (ℓ, Etarget): ν is an integer when the state with ν nodes sits exactly at Etarget. Each point also carries its Wildermuth number G = 2n + ℓ (n = nearest integer to ν) and the bound-state counts Nb(ℓ). By Levinson's theorem Nb(ℓ) = [δℓ(0) − δℓ(∞)]/π for the real potential.

Refitted at each V₀
Classes fitted at each V₀:
Fill the registry (tab 7) and press Run scan. The scan starts at the grid point nearest the current V₀ (left panel) and continues outward in both directions; each fit starts from the extrapolation of its neighbours. Cost per point: one fit (typically 15–70 registry evaluations of the fitted classes with three free parameters; measured 16–48 on the α+²⁰⁸Pb 40 MeV and α+¹⁶O 32 MeV pseudo-data, more far from a family) plus one evaluation of all classes.

Each class is evaluated at the potential fitted at that V₀. A class that is not fitted but has a sharp minimum is the one that selects the family.

Minima (families)

Δχ² is measured from the best minimum of this scan. The column “excluded by” names the fitted class whose χ² rises most from the best minimum to this one, which is the source of Δχ². It also names the class not fitted that would separate the two minima most. Show plots the band spectrum and band-head wave function of that family; Use loads its potential into the left panel.

Method and limitations

  • Profile fit. At each V₀ a Levenberg–Marquardt fit is run in the scaled coordinates of tab 9 (V₀, W₀ logarithmic). The Jacobian uses forward differences with steps 10⁻⁵ (relative) and Broyden updates. A fresh Jacobian is taken whenever the gain ratio falls below ¼, and convergence is declared on a fresh Jacobian when the Gauss–Newton step predicts a decrease below 10⁻⁴ + 10⁻⁷ χ². A trial step that loses a row (state not found) is rejected.
  • Continuation. Each fit starts from the linear extrapolation of the two previous optima on its branch, or from the Igo-line predictor for rV at the first step. Polish refits non-converged points from their neighbours' optima. Refine performs successive parabolic interpolation in V₀ around each minimum, with a full fit at each trial.
  • Local minima. Wide-angle elastic χ² surfaces are multimodal in (rV, aV). The profile therefore follows the valley connected to the starting potential, and a fit from a distant start can end in a local minimum. Start from a good fit, and check suspicious points in the point table.
  • Labels. ν comes from Sturm-count bisection for a bound Etarget; for an unbound target it comes from gamow.html's narrow-resonance depth fit, which is valid for ℓ < 7. Nb(ℓ) counts bound states at E → 0⁻ with the real potential at E = 0. Pauli: G < GW is Pauli-forbidden, G = GW is the Wildermuth family, and G > GW is an excited (deeper) family.
  • Admissibility. Δχ² ≤ threshold relative to the best minimum of the same scan. The parameters that are not refitted stay at the left-panel values, so this is a profile in a subspace; Stage 5 adds the full profile likelihood.

Hierarchical and global fit

One potential is fitted to every selected registry class. The sequential fit follows the order N → V₀ → rV → aV → β → cM → W. Its N step places the band head (ℓ, n) of the registry at its energy, which fixes the family. Each later step adds one parameter and the class assigned to it by the one-to-one assignment of tab 9. In the cumulative mode (default) step k refits all parameters added so far to all classes added so far, together with the band-head energy of step N; in the one-parameter mode it fits the new parameter alone. This gives starting values and the physical reading of the fit. The global fit then frees all selected parameters together (Levenberg–Marquardt). Its covariance comes from a central-difference Jacobian at the optimum, with nuisance factors profiled and the model-error floors of tab 7 added in quadrature.

Free parameters
Classes fitted:
Fill the registry (tab 7), select the free parameters and press Plan, then the sequential and the global fit. The global fit starts from the sequential result when there is one, otherwise from the left panel.

Sequential plan

Class: the class assigned to the parameter by the one-to-one assignment (tab 9), editable. The share is that class's fraction of the parameter's variance. Leak: the response of the step's class to a 1σ change of a later parameter, relative to its response to the step parameter itself. Sequential fixing reproduces the global fit when every leak is ≪ 1, i.e. when S is nearly block-triangular in this order. A one-to-one class with less than 10 % of the parameter's variance is replaced by the parameter's best class; a step that makes rows of other classes lose their model value is reverted.

Sequential steps

Parameters

σ: square root of the covariance diagonal; with the Birge option, scaled by √(χ²/ν) when that is above 1. Shift: (sequential − global)/σ, the cross-talk the sequential fit leaves. Profile: the Δχ² = 1 interval of the profile likelihood. MCMC: posterior median and central 68 % interval (uniform prior inside the box).

Correlation matrix (global fit)

χ² per class at the global optimum

Profile likelihoods

The chosen parameter is fixed on a grid around the global optimum and all other free parameters are refitted (continuation from the neighbouring point). The grid is extended until Δχ² = 1 is crossed on both sides, and each interval end is refined by a fit at the interpolated crossing (two passes at most). The curves are drawn against (p − p̂)/σ, so a linear problem gives the parabola x² on every curve. A profile point below the global χ² means that the global fit stopped short of the minimum.

Profiled parameters

MCMC (affine-invariant ensemble sampler)

The sampler uses the stretch move of Goodman and Weare (2010), a = 2, on the scaled coordinates of the free parameters. The target is exp(−χ²/2) times a uniform prior in the physical parameters inside the box of the fit. Points where a registry row has no model value have zero density. Walkers start from the global-fit covariance times the spread factor. The acceptance fraction should lie between about 0.2 and 0.5. The run should be ≳ 50 integrated autocorrelation times τ long after burn-in, because shorter chains under-estimate the tails. Use MCMC to see curved or multimodal valleys (such as the Igo valley of elastic-only data) that the covariance cannot represent.

Propagation: invariants and prediction bands

Linear: σ² = gᵀCg with g the central-difference gradient of the quantity. Sampled: the same quantity over parameter sets drawn from the covariance (Gaussian in the scaled coordinates, truncated to the box), or over MCMC samples. Bands: 16–84 % of the sampled model curves. VN(R) is taken at the best-fit strong-absorption radius, held fixed for all samples; this is the quantity elastic scattering determines best.

Closure test (coverage)

Truth: the potential in the left panel. Design: the selected classes of the registry (their kinds, energies and angles; the values are replaced). For each realisation, pseudo-data are drawn with the Stage 1 noise model (5 % on cross sections, 10 % on widths, ANC and B(E2), 50 keV on energies). The global fit then starts from the truth perturbed by the given relative amount, and the pull (p̂ − ptrue)/σ is recorded. If the covariance is right, about 68.3 % of the pulls satisfy |pull| ≤ 1; with N realisations the binomial 1σ is √(0.683 · 0.317/N). The joint test counts realisations with (p̂ − ptrue)ᵀC⁻¹(p̂ − ptrue) below the 68.3 % quantile of χ² with the number of free parameters. With the floors switched off, σ is the pseudo-data noise alone, as appropriate for an exact model. A fit that ends with p < 10⁻⁴ (a local minimum reached from the perturbed start) is refitted from the truth, so the coverage refers to the global minimum; the number of such local minima is reported.

Method and limitations

  • Covariance. C = (JᵀJ)⁻¹ in the scaled coordinates (V₀, W₀ logarithmic), from a central-difference Jacobian (steps 10⁻⁴ relative) with a step-halving check. Nuisance groups are projected out (profiled), so C is the covariance profiled over the normalisations and the free preformation factor. It is a local, linear quantity: along the Igo valley of elastic-only data it is not a valid description, so use the profiles or MCMC there.
  • Correlation is not ambiguity. A bound or quasi-bound energy constrains a line in (V₀, rV) nearly parallel to the elastic Igo line. Adding it therefore shrinks σ(V₀) by an order of magnitude and selects the family, while |ρ(V₀, rV)| stays near 1. The widths and the family scan (tab 11) measure the removal of the ambiguity; ρ alone does not.
  • Sequential fit. In the one-parameter mode each step fits one parameter to its class with all others held; with strong cross-talk (leak ≥ 1) its result can lie in another basin of χ² (α+¹⁶O: see the Stage 5 report). The cumulative mode refits the earlier parameters at every step and is the default. Either way the sequential fit is a starting point; the global fit gives the result.
  • Cost. One registry evaluation costs about 0.07 s (α+²⁰⁸Pb, one elastic energy), 0.45 s (two energies + Qα + Γ) or 2.3 s (α+¹⁶O, full design) in V8. A global fit takes up to 100 + 60·np evaluations (typically far fewer); MCMC needs walkers × steps evaluations, and a 30-realisation closure test about 30 global fits. Everything runs in one Web Worker, without parallelism.
  • Box. rV, rW ∈ [0.3, 3] fm, aV ∈ [0.2, 3] fm, aW ∈ [0.1, 3] fm, V₀ ∈ [1, 2000] MeV, W₀ ∈ [0.01, 500] MeV, EW ∈ [0, 200] MeV, ΔW ∈ [0.1, 200] MeV. A parameter that ends on a bound is flagged; its σ then has no meaning.

Benchmarks with real data

Each benchmark builds the observable registry from data bundled in this file, retrieved at build time by tools/fetch_data.py. The sources are ENSDF adopted levels and γ rays (IAEA LiveChart), EXFOR elastic angular distributions (exfortables_py) and NUBASE2020 (gamow.html), with the bands and data sets listed below. The chain then runs the family scan (tab 11), selects the admissible minimum of the Wildermuth family, and performs the sequential and global fits (tab 12) with the benchmark's free parameters. It finally evaluates the acceptance criteria of the prompt. Every step can also be run by hand in tabs 7, 11 and 12; the benchmark only sets their inputs.

Choose a benchmark and press Run all, or run the steps one by one. Cost: α+²⁰⁸Pb and α+⁴⁰Ca take tens of minutes, α+¹⁶O about an hour in one Web Worker.

Acceptance

The criteria of the prompt:

  • Fitted and predicted rows. Rows marked predicted (the ²¹²Po excited yrast states, kept in the registry with include off) are not fitted. They are scored with the band factor fitted to the other members of the band.
  • Energies within σ_th: |E_model − E_exp| ≤ σ_eff, where σ_eff is the data uncertainty with the model-error floor of tab 7 (100 keV) added in quadrature.
  • Widths within their uncertainties: |z| ≤ 1 after the band's reduced-width factor θ²_G (one factor per band, profiled, so only width ratios within a band are tested).
  • B(E2) within its uncertainty (σ_eff includes the 10 % floor; LiveChart gives no B(E2) uncertainties).
  • Elastic χ² per point per data set.
  • Single admissible family (Δχ² ≤ threshold) in the family scan.

Closure coverage is a property of the method and the design; it is tested in tab 12 and in the Stage 5 report.

Report

The report collects the system, the data and their provenance, the family scan, the fitted potential with σ, the correlation matrix, χ² per class, profile intervals, invariants and the acceptance tables. The HTML report embeds the figures of tabs 11 and 12 when the browser can render them (Plotly.toImage); the Markdown report has the tables only; the JSON file holds the potential with its covariance and every table.

Bundled data and provenance

Method and limitations

  • Bands. The band members, their Wildermuth G and the EXFOR data sets of each benchmark are fixed in the engine (BENCH in the wb-bench block) and listed above. Change them by editing the registry (tab 7) after step 1.
  • Family scan. V₀ is stepped over 60–300 MeV with rV, aV, W₀ (and cM for two parities) refitted to all rows, as in tab 11. The prescribed node numbers of the energy rows make the scan discriminate between families. The global fit then starts from the lowest point of the Wildermuth family.
  • Global fit. All benchmark parameters are freed together (tab 12). A single fit can end in a local minimum; the family scan and the profile flag this.
  • Cost. Everything runs in one Web Worker; the α+¹⁶O chain is the longest.

In-browser self-check

Recomputes reference quantities in this browser and compares them with values from an independent solver: a Python finite-difference and Numerov code with mpmath Coulomb functions that shares no code with the engine.
